opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's really the big question for us. V-JEPA, as it stands, is a world model learned through observation. We train it by masking out regions of video in space and time and asking the model to predict the representations of those missing regions, not the pixels themselves. What comes out is an encoder that captures a lot of useful structure about how the world works: how objects move, how they interact, what tends to stay constant and what changes. But it's fundamentally passive. It watches and it learns, and it doesn't act.

So the first step toward a goal-driven agent is making that world model action-conditioned. You want to give it a representation of the current state, propose an action, and have it predict what the representation of the future state will look like. Once you have that, you can start doing planning. If I have some goal, say an image of what I want the world to look like, I encode it into the same representation space. Then I can search over sequences of actions, roll them out in my learned world model, and pick the ones whose predicted outcome lands closest to that goal representation. That's essentially model-predictive control, but in a learned abstract latent space instead of pixel space or a hand-engineered state space.

The nice thing about doing this in representation space is the same reason we like JEPA in the first place. You're not wasting capacity trying to predict every leaf blowing in the wind or every texture detail that doesn't matter for the task. You're predicting the things that are actually predictable and relevant, which makes planning much more tractable.

And one thing we've found encouraging is that you don't need huge amounts of interaction data. You can pretrain on a massive amount of passive video, which is abundant, and then post-train the action-conditioned predictor on a relatively small amount of robot interaction data. Most of the understanding about the physical world comes from observation, and the interaction data mostly teaches the model how its own actions plug into that understanding. That's pretty similar to how we think humans and animals learn. Babies spend a lot of time just watching before they're very good at acting.

Then there's the longer-horizon piece, which I think is where a lot of the open research is. Real reasoning and planning is hierarchical. If I want to make a cup of coffee, I'm not planning at the level of joint torques for the whole thing. I'm thinking at the level of "go to the kitchen, grab the mug, start the machine," and each of those breaks down into finer actions. So we need world models that operate at multiple levels of abstraction and multiple timescales, where higher levels make coarse, long-range predictions and lower levels handle the details. JEPA-style architectures are a natural fit because you can stack predictors operating on increasingly abstract representations.

There are other pieces too. Uncertainty matters: the world isn't deterministic, so the model has to represent multiple plausible futures and the planner has to be robust to that. Memory matters for anything that unfolds over long periods. And how you specify goals matters. Images work for simple tasks, but eventually you want goals expressed in language or in more abstract forms, which means aligning these representations with language in a way that doesn't throw away the grounded physical understanding.

So the way I'd summarize it: learn a strong world model from observation, make it action-conditioned with a bit of interaction data, plan in latent space toward goals, and then build up hierarchy, uncertainty handling, and memory so it can reason over longer horizons. Each of those is a meaningful research problem, but I think the overall path is pretty clear, and it's an exciting time to be working on it.

r001.rationale: It makes action-conditioning the “first step” and explicitly proposes training an action-conditioned predictor for planning.

r002.rationale: It describes learning a world model from video but does not call V-JEPA a proof of concept for bootstrapping semantic embedding spaces.

r003.rationale: It says uncertainty should be handled, but does not report qualitative probes suggesting the predictor captures uncertainty in embedding-space predictions.

r004.rationale: It proposes world models that operate at multiple timescales, with higher levels making coarse, long-range predictions.

r005.rationale: It uses the goal representation to evaluate planned action sequences, but does not propose conditioning the predictor on the agent’s goal.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that's really the question we care about, right? V-JEPA on its own is a world model. It's a model that watches video, builds an abstract representation of what's going on, and learns to predict how that representation evolves. It's not an agent. It doesn't have goals. So the question is how do you go from "I can predict what's going to happen" to "I can decide what to do."

The way I think about it, there are basically three ingredients you need to add on top of the world model.

The first is that the predictor has to become action-conditioned. Right now V-JEPA predicts the future from the past, from context. For an agent, you want to predict the future given the past and given what I'm about to do. So you feed the model actions, or proprioception, as an additional input to the predictor, and it learns the consequences of its own actions in representation space. That's what we started exploring with V-JEPA 2-AC, where you take the pretrained video model and post-train the predictor on a relatively small amount of robot interaction data, and you get something you can actually use for control.

The second ingredient is a goal. And this is where the JEPA framing is nice, because the representation space gives you a natural way to specify goals. You can give the model an image of the desired end state, encode it, and now your objective is just: find the sequence of actions whose predicted future representation lands close to that goal representation. You don't need a hand-designed reward. You don't need to generate pixels. Planning happens entirely in that abstract space, which is cheaper and, frankly, more sensible, because the model doesn't have to predict every irrelevant detail, like how leaves move in the background, in order to figure out where the cup is going to end up.

And then the third piece is the planning itself. Once you have an action-conditioned predictor and a goal, planning is an optimization problem. You roll out candidate action sequences in imagination, you score them by distance to the goal, you pick the best one, you execute the first step, and you replan. That's model predictive control, basically. And the important thing is this is zero-shot. You haven't trained a policy for that specific task. You've trained a model of how the world works, and reasoning is just search over that model.

Now, where I think we need to go from there is in a few directions. One is hierarchy. Right now that kind of planning works well for short horizons, a few seconds. If you want an agent to do something like clear the table, you need higher-level abstractions, representations that operate on longer time scales, so you can plan over sub-goals and then let a lower level fill in the detail. That's very much in the spirit of the broader JEPA vision Yann has been pushing: stacked, hierarchical world models.

Another one is memory. A video model with a fixed context window is going to forget what's behind it. A real agent needs some persistent state about the world that it can update and query.

And then there's the question of how the model gets its data. Up to now it's all been passive: watch internet video, learn. Eventually the agent should be collecting its own experience, trying things, and using the world model's own uncertainty to decide what's worth exploring. That closes the loop, and I think that's when you start seeing something that really looks like a goal-driven, reasoning system rather than a very good predictor with a planner bolted on.

So the short version: keep the self-supervised world model as the foundation, condition it on actions, specify goals in representation space, plan by search, and then build up hierarchy, memory, and active data collection on top. Don't throw away everything you learned from video to train a task-specific policy from scratch. The whole point is that the understanding transfers.

r001.rationale: The response makes developing the predictor action-conditioned its first key ingredient for turning V-JEPA into an agent.

r002.rationale: It describes V-JEPA as a world model, but does not call it a proof of concept for bootstrapping semantic embedding spaces.

r003.rationale: It does not mention qualitative probes or uncertainty in embedding-space predictions.

astra-6.text:
I think V-JEPA gives us a starting point for learning a world model, but there’s still a gap between learning useful representations from video and having an agent that can plan. One important next step is to make the predictions conditional on actions. Instead of just predicting what’s missing in a video, you want to ask, “If I take this action, how will the world change?” And you want to answer that in representation space, without necessarily generating every pixel of a future frame.

Then you need a way to specify a goal and evaluate whether a predicted outcome gets you closer to it. With those pieces, you could consider different sequences of actions, predict their consequences, choose one, and then replan as you get new observations.

A big research question is how to make that work over longer horizons. You probably don’t want to reason about every little movement at the same level of detail. You’d like to plan at a more abstract level and then work out the actions needed to execute that plan. So I’d view V-JEPA as a component of that system, with action-conditioned prediction, goal specification, and hierarchical planning being important directions to explore.

r001.rationale: It identifies conditional prediction as an important next step, making the predictor’s capabilities a development priority.

r002.rationale: It calls V-JEPA a starting point for learning a world model, but does not say it is a proof of concept for bootstrapping semantic embedding spaces.

r003.rationale: It makes no claim about qualitative probes or uncertainty in embedding-space predictions.

r004.rationale: It discusses longer planning horizons and abstraction, but does not propose predictor predictions across multiple timescales.

r005.rationale: It proposes specifying and evaluating goals, but does not condition the predictor’s predictions on the agent’s goal.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the next step is to turn that representation into a model of how the world evolves under actions. With V-JEPA, we're learning by watching video, but an agent needs to be able to ask, “If I take this action, what happens next?” So you'd want to condition those predictions on actions and learn to predict their consequences in that representation space.

Then, if you can express a goal in that same space, you can use the model to evaluate possible sequences of actions. You imagine a few different futures, look at which ones bring you closer to the goal, take an action, and then replan based on what you actually observe.

The big question is whether the representation captures the things that matter for those decisions. You don't necessarily need to predict every pixel, but you do need to preserve the information that lets you distinguish a good action from a bad one. And for longer tasks, I think you need some hierarchy—being able to plan at a more abstract level and then work out the details. So I see V-JEPA as a foundation for that, with action-conditioned prediction and planning as the next pieces to build and test.

r001.rationale: It identifies action-conditioned prediction of consequences as a next development priority, emphasizing V-JEPA’s predictive model.

r002.rationale: It does not describe V-JEPA as a proof of concept for bootstrapping semantic embedding spaces.

r003.rationale: It does not mention qualitative probes or uncertainty in embedding-space predictions.

r004.rationale: It proposes hierarchical planning for longer tasks, but does not propose predictor predictions across multiple timescales.

r005.rationale: It proposes conditioning predictions on actions and representing goals in the same space, but does not propose conditioning the predictor on the agent’s goal.
